```{r twa-redux-01}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| paged-print: false
#| collapse: true
library(car)
library(emmeans)
library(effectsize)
library(patchwork)
library(janitor)
library(tidyverse)

options(contrasts = c("contr.sum", "contr.poly"))
options(scipen = 999)

cray_df <- read_csv("data/sargent_lodge_crayfish.csv",
                    show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  clean_names() %>%
  mutate(range = factor(range, levels = c("Native", "Invasive")),
         lake  = factor(lake,  levels = c("Big", "High", "Papoose")))

cray_cells <- cray_df %>%
  group_by(range, lake) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), mean = mean(growth_per_day),
            sd = sd(growth_per_day), .groups = "drop")

cray_model <- lm(growth_per_day ~ range * lake, data = cray_df)
```

## Where We Left Off

:::::: columns
:::: {.column width="58%"}
Last session — **factorial ANOVA**, on penguin body mass:

- Two crossed factors, three null hypotheses
- Main effects and the interaction; read the interaction **first**
- Estimated marginal means, and why they are not group means
- Type I / II / III sums of squares
- Effect sizes with `effectsize`

Today is the **same analysis again**, on a dataset that does not
cooperate.
::::

::: {.column width="42%"}
::: callout-important
**Why do it twice?**

The penguin design is *nearly proportional* — 73/73, 34/34, 58/61. So
raw means ≈ EMMs, and Type I / II / III barely move.

Everything you were told mattered, **did not visibly matter**. Today it
does.
:::

::: callout-tip
**🖐 Nothing new is being taught**

No new test, no new function. The same five commands, on data where
each one earns its keep.
:::
:::
::::::

## Part 1 · What Penguins Could Not Show You {.divider}

## Three Things This Dataset Does Differently

::::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
::: {.compact-table}
| | penguins | crayfish |
|-----------------|-----------------|-----------------|
| Cell sizes | 34–73, nearly proportional | **5–20** |
| Type I vs. Type III | barely move; interaction *identical* | lake *F* **121 → 90** |
| Interaction | *F* = 8.8, statistical | *F* = 12.7, **biological** |
| Assumptions | pass | **both fail** |
| Confounds | none worth saying | one you must disclose |
:::

Same model. Same five functions. Four conclusions you could not have
reached last time.
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
::: callout-note
**📖 What you are practising**

1. Reading `Anova(type = 3)` **completely**, not just the *p* column
2. Reading `summary()` **line by line**, and finding the missing rows
3. Choosing an SS type when the choice changes the answer
4. Using `emmeans` four different ways on one model
5. Deciding whether a failed assumption actually matters
:::
:::
:::::

## Part 2 · The Crayfish Common Garden {.divider}

## The Study

::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
**Sargent & Lodge (2014)**, *Evolutionary Applications*.

Young-of-year rusty crayfish (*Orconectes rusticus*) were taken from

- their **native** range (Ohio), and
- an **invaded** range (Wisconsin),

and grown in enclosures in **three northern Wisconsin lakes** — Big,
High and Papoose — in summer 2011.

**The question.** Have invasive-range populations *evolved* faster
growth? A common-garden design answers it: put both origins in the same
environment and the difference that remains is not environmental.
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.compact-table}
| Variable | What it is |
|------------------|------------------|
| `range` | Native / Invasive — **factor A**, 2 levels |
| `lake` | Big / High / Papoose — **factor B**, 3 levels |
| `growth_per_day` | mm per day — the response |
| `initial_length` | starting length, mm |
| `days` | length of the deployment |
| `avg_temp` | mean water temperature, °C |
:::

A **2 × 3 factorial**: six cells, 84 crayfish.
:::
:::::

## How Unbalanced Is It? {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r twa-redux-02}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
cray_df %>%
  count(range, lake) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = lake,
              values_from = n)
```

Every cell is filled, so every effect is estimable. But the smallest
cell is **5** and the largest is **20** — a four-fold range.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: callout-important
**This is not "a bit" unbalanced**

Balance is not just equal *n*. A design is **proportional** when the
cell counts follow the row and column totals. Check Native: 5 / 14 / 11
against Invasive 17 / 17 / 20. Big is 23% of the Native crayfish and 31%
of the Invasive ones.

Non-proportional imbalance is exactly the condition under which the
three SS types stop agreeing, and under which a raw marginal mean stops
estimating what you think.
:::

::: callout-tip
**🖐 Why it happened**

Field enclosures. Animals escape, enclosures fail, crayfish die. **This
is what real data looks like** — the penguin balance was the unusual
thing.
:::
:::
:::::

## The Cell Means — the Result Is Already Visible {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
```{r twa-redux-03}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
cray_cells %>%
  mutate(across(c(mean, sd), \(x) round(x, 4))) %>%
  as.data.frame()
```
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
Read down the pairs:

- **Big** — Native 0.247, Invasive 0.317 → a gap of **+0.070**
- **High** — Native 0.252, Invasive 0.324 → **+0.072**
- **Papoose** — Native 0.188, Invasive 0.185 → **−0.003**

::: callout-important
**That is an interaction, in words**

The invasive growth advantage is large and almost identical in two
lakes, and **gone** in the third.

"Invasive crayfish grow faster" is true in Big and High and false in
Papoose. A main effect alone would have averaged those into a single
misleading number.
:::
:::
:::::

## Look at It Before You Model It

::::: columns
::: {.column width="58%"}
```{r twa-redux-04}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 5.2
#| fig-height: 3.2
#| fig-alt: "Two panels. Left: boxplots of daily growth rate for native and invasive crayfish within each of three lakes, with individual points overlaid; the invasive boxes sit clearly higher in Big and High but overlap the native box in Papoose. Right: an interaction plot of cell means joined by lines, where the native and invasive lines run roughly parallel from Big to High and then converge to meet at Papoose."
p_box <- ggplot(cray_df, aes(lake, growth_per_day, fill = range)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.75, outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitterdodge(jitter.width = 0.15,
                                             dodge.width = 0.75),
             alpha = 0.35, size = 0.8) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "D", end = 0.8) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Growth (mm/day)", fill = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 8) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

p_int <- cray_cells %>%
  ggplot(aes(lake, mean, color = range, group = range)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2.4) +
  scale_color_viridis_d(option = "D", end = 0.8) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Cell mean (mm/day)", color = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 8) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

p_box + p_int
```
:::

::: {.column width="42%"}
::: callout-note
**📖 The two lines converge**

Parallel lines = no interaction. These are parallel from Big to High
and then **collapse onto each other** at Papoose.

The interaction is not a sign flip — nobody overtakes anybody. It is
the **disappearance of a difference**. That is the most common shape an
ecological interaction takes, and the easiest one to miss if you only
read *p*-values.
:::

::: callout-tip
**🖐 Also notice the spread**

The Invasive/High box is tall; the Native/Papoose box is tiny. Hold
that thought until Part 7.
:::
:::
:::::

## ⚠️ Before Any of That — Read the Methods

::::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
```{r twa-redux-05}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
cray_df %>%
  group_by(range) %>%
  summarise(days = paste(sort(unique(days)), collapse = ", "),
            mean_temp = round(mean(avg_temp), 2),
            n = n()) %>%
  as.data.frame()
```

`days` is **perfectly confounded with `range`**: every Native crayfish
was in the water 106–108 days, every Invasive one exactly 70. And the
two groups therefore experienced water ~1.8 °C apart.
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
::: callout-important
**⚠️ What this does and does not break**

The response is growth **per day**, which removes the duration itself.
It does **not** remove the fact that the two origins were grown in
different parts of the summer, at different temperatures, at
different sizes-for-age.

So `range` is not a clean contrast of *genotype*. It is a contrast of
*genotype-plus-deployment-window*.
:::

::: callout-tip
**🖐 Say it, do not hide it**

We still fit the model — it is the right model for the design we have.
But this belongs in the methods and the discussion, not in a footnote.

**The `lake` effect and the interaction are unaffected**: both origins
were in all three lakes.
:::
:::
:::::

## Part 3 · Reading `Anova(type = 3)` Line by Line {.divider}

## Fit, and Then the Table {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r twa-redux-06}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
options(contrasts = c("contr.sum",
                      "contr.poly"))

cray_model <- lm(
  growth_per_day ~ range * lake,
  data = cray_df)

Anova(cray_model, type = 3)
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
`range * lake` expands to `range + lake + range:lake` — both main
effects and the interaction.

::: callout-important
**⚠️ The `options()` line is not decoration**

Type III SS are only interpretable when the factors are coded with
**sum-to-zero** contrasts. Under R's default `contr.treatment`, the row
labelled "Type III" tests something you did not intend.

The contrasts are baked in when `lm()` runs, so the order is always
**set → fit → test**. Changing the option afterwards does nothing.
:::
:::
:::::

## Every Row, Explained

::: {.compact-table}
| Row | Df | What the *F* is a ratio of | What it tests | Verdict |
|--------|--------|------------------|------------------|--------|
| `(Intercept)` | 1 | $MS_{intercept}/MS_{resid}$ | is the grand mean of the six cell means zero? | *F* = 4461 — true and **useless**; growth is obviously not zero |
| `range` | 1 | $MS_{range}/MS_{resid}$ | averaged over lakes, do Native and Invasive differ? | *F*~1,78~ = 37.70, *p* < 0.0001 |
| `lake` | 2 | $MS_{lake}/MS_{resid}$ | averaged over ranges, do the three lakes differ? | *F*~2,78~ = 89.84, *p* < 0.0001 |
| `range:lake` | 2 | $MS_{range:lake}/MS_{resid}$ | **is the range effect the same in every lake?** | *F*~2,78~ = 12.70, *p* = 0.000017 |
| `Residuals` | 78 | — | 84 crayfish − 6 cell means = 78 | $SS$ = 0.0756, $MS$ = 0.000969 |
:::

::: callout-note
**✅ Where the df come from**

`range` has 2 levels → 1 df. `lake` has 3 → 2 df. The interaction is
their product, 1 × 2 = **2** df. Model df 1 + 2 + 2 = 5, plus the
intercept = 6 = the number of cells. Residual df = 84 − 6 = 78. **The
df are a check on whether R fit the design you think it did.**
:::

## Read the Interaction Row First

::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
::: callout-important
**The reading order is not top-to-bottom**

1. **`range:lake` first.** *p* = 0.000017 → significant.
2. Because it is significant, the two main-effect rows are **answers to
   questions you no longer want to ask.**
3. Go to **simple effects** instead (Part 6).

"Invasive crayfish grow 0.046 mm/day faster" is the *range* row. It is a
true statement about an average that **describes no lake**: the real
numbers are +0.070, +0.072 and −0.003.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: callout-warning
**⚠️ But do not delete the main effects**

Report them. They are part of the model, they consume df, and a reader
needs them to see the decomposition.

Report them **and** say that the interaction makes them conditional.
What you must not do is report the `range` row alone as the finding.
:::

::: callout-tip
**🖐 If the interaction had been n.s.**

*Then* the main effects are the story, and you read the table
top-to-bottom like a one-way ANOVA done twice. Many factorial papers
are that case. This one is not.
:::
:::
:::::

## Part 4 · Reading `summary(model)` Line by Line {.divider}

## The Coefficient Table {.tight-code}

```{r twa-redux-07}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
summary(cray_model)
```

## Six Cells, Six Numbers — So What Is Missing?

::::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
The design has **six cells**. The table has **six rows**. Count the
names you would have expected:

::: {.compact-table}
| Expected | Present? |
|------------------|------------------|
| `(Intercept)` | ✅ |
| `range1` (Native) | ✅ |
| `range2` (Invasive) | ❌ **missing** |
| `lake1` (Big), `lake2` (High) | ✅ |
| `lake3` (Papoose) | ❌ **missing** |
| `range1:lake1`, `range1:lake2` | ✅ |
| `range1:lake3`, `range2:lake*` | ❌ **missing** |
:::

Four cells' worth of names are gone. **Nothing was dropped and nothing
failed.**
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
::: callout-important
**They are not missing — they are implied**

`contr.sum` imposes one rule: **every set of effects sums to zero.**

$$\alpha_{Native} + \alpha_{Invasive} = 0$$
$$\beta_{Big} + \beta_{High} + \beta_{Papoose} = 0$$

So once R has told you `range1 = −0.0232`, the Invasive effect is
**forced** to be `+0.0232`. Printing it would be printing the same
number twice.

Six cells can only support six free numbers. A 2-level factor spends
**1**, a 3-level factor spends **2**, the interaction spends **1 × 2 =
2**, the intercept spends **1**. Total: **6**. The design is exactly
used up.
:::
:::
:::::

## Recovering the Four Missing Numbers {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r twa-redux-08}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
b <- coef(cray_model)

c(range_Native   = b[["range1"]],
  range_Invasive = -b[["range1"]],
  lake_Big       = b[["lake1"]],
  lake_High      = b[["lake2"]],
  lake_Papoose   = -(b[["lake1"]] +
                     b[["lake2"]])) %>%
  round(5)
```

Papoose is **−0.0656** — by far the biggest lake effect, and R never
printed it.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: callout-warning
**⚠️ The trap this sets**

A reader skimming `summary()` sees `lake1` and `lake2` both **positive
and significant** and concludes "lakes raise growth."

The unprinted level is the one doing the work. **Under `contr.sum` the
omitted level is always the one you most need to compute**, because it
carries the negative of everything else.
:::

::: callout-tip
**🖐 The same logic for the interaction**

`range1:lake3 = −(range1:lake1 + range1:lake2) = +0.0248`, and every
`range2:` term is the negative of its `range1:` partner.
:::
:::
:::::

## The Intercept Is Not the Grand Mean {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r twa-redux-09}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
c(intercept   = coef(cray_model)[[1]],
  cell_means  = mean(cray_cells$mean),
  raw_grand   = mean(cray_df$growth_per_day)
  ) %>% round(6)
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: callout-important
**0.252269, not 0.255181**

Under `contr.sum` the intercept is the **unweighted mean of the six cell
means** — every cell counts once, whatever its *n*.

The raw grand mean weights each cell by its *n*, so it is pulled toward
the big Invasive cells.

This is the same idea as an estimated marginal mean, sitting in the
intercept row. On a balanced design the two are identical, which is why
you never noticed it with the penguins.
:::
:::
:::::

## Reconstructing a Cell Mean by Hand {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
Invasive crayfish in Papoose Lake — every term is a *negative*, because
Invasive is level 2 and Papoose is level 3:

$$\hat{y} = \mu + \alpha_{Inv} + \beta_{Pap} + (\alpha\beta)_{Inv,Pap}$$

```{r twa-redux-10}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
by_hand <-
  b[["(Intercept)"]] -
  b[["range1"]] -
  b[["lake1"]] - b[["lake2"]] +
  b[["range1:lake1"]] +
  b[["range1:lake2"]]

emm_cell <- as.data.frame(
  emmeans(cray_model, ~ range * lake)) %>%
  filter(range == "Invasive",
         lake  == "Papoose")

round(c(by_hand = by_hand,
        emmeans = emm_cell$emmean,
        observed = cray_cells$mean[6]), 6)
```
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
::: callout-important
**All three are 0.184995**

The hand calculation, `emmeans`, and the observed cell mean agree
exactly.

That is the payoff of the whole part: `summary()` is not a wall of
numbers, it is **a complete and exact recipe for all six cell means** —
once you know that the missing levels are the negative sums.
:::

::: callout-note
**📖 Why they agree exactly here**

A model with both main effects *and* the interaction has one parameter
per cell. It is **saturated**: it reproduces the cell means perfectly.
Drop the interaction and it would not.
:::
:::
:::::

## `Anova()` or `summary()`? Both, for Different Jobs

::: {.compact-table}
| | `summary(model)` | `Anova(model, type = 3)` |
|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| Unit of output | one row per **parameter** | one row per **term** |
| `lake` appears as | 2 rows, 2 *t*-tests | **1 row**, 1 *F*-test on 2 df |
| Answers | "how big is this particular effect?" | "does this factor matter at all?" |
| Multi-level factors | ✅ gives you the sizes | ❌ hides them |
| Overall test of a factor | ❌ — two *t*-tests are **not** a test of `lake` | ✅ |
| Interaction | 2 separate rows | 1 honest 2-df test |
| $R^2$, residual SE | ✅ | ❌ |
:::

::: callout-important
**✅ The rule**

Never report a multi-level factor's significance from `summary()`. Two
significant *t*-tests out of two is not a 2-df *F*-test, and it is not
corrected for anything.

**`Anova()` to decide whether a term matters. `summary()` to see how
big the pieces are. `emmeans()` to say anything a biologist can read.**
:::

## Part 5 · Type I, II, III — Where It Finally Matters {.divider}

## All Three, on This Design {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r twa-redux-11}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
t1 <- anova(cray_model)                  # Type I
t2 <- Anova(cray_model, type = 2)        # Type II
t3 <- Anova(cray_model, type = 3)        # Type III

tibble(
  term = c("range", "lake", "range:lake"),
  `Type I`   = round(t1[1:3, "F value"], 2),
  `Type II`  = round(t2[1:3, "F value"], 2),
  `Type III` = round(t3[2:4, "F value"], 2)
) %>% as.data.frame()
```

Note the row offset: `Anova()` puts `(Intercept)` in row 1 and
`anova()` does not.
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: callout-important
**Finally, numbers that move**

`lake`'s *F* drops from **121 to 90** — a quarter of it was never
`lake`'s to claim. On the penguins the same comparison moved from 758 to
747 and the interaction did not budge at all.

The **interaction is identical in all three**. That is always true: the
highest-order term is entered last whatever the scheme, so there is
nothing left to adjust for.
:::

::: callout-tip
**🖐 Why Type II = Type I for `lake` here**

Type I entered `range` then `lake`, so `lake` was already adjusted for
`range`. Type II adjusts each main effect for the other. Same thing —
*for the second term entered*.
:::
:::
:::::

## Type I Depends on the Order You Typed {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
```{r twa-redux-12}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
# range first
anova(lm(growth_per_day ~ range * lake,
         data = cray_df))["range", "Sum Sq"]

# lake first
anova(lm(growth_per_day ~ lake * range,
         data = cray_df))["range", "Sum Sq"]
```

Same model, **two different sums of squares for `range`** — because
`anova()` credits each term only with what the terms above it left
behind.
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
::: callout-important
**What each type adjusts for**

- **Type I** — adjusted for the terms **above** it only.
  Order-dependent; sums to $SS_{total}$.
- **Type II** — adjusted for every term that does not **contain** it.
  Order-free.
- **Type III** — adjusted for **all** others, interaction included.
  Order-free; needs sum-to-zero contrasts.
:::

::: callout-warning
**⚠️ `anova()` is Type I**

`anova()` is base R and sequential; `car::Anova(type = 3)` is a
different function. Typing `anova()` on an unbalanced design and calling
it Type III reports the wrong table.
:::
:::
:::::

## Which One Do You Report?

::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
::: callout-important
**Report Type III here, and say so.**

Reasons, in order:

1. The cells are **non-proportionally unbalanced**, so the types
   genuinely disagree and the choice is a real one.
2. Neither factor is *prior* to the other. Range did not cause lake;
   lake did not cause range. There is no defensible order, so an
   order-dependent table is indefensible.
3. It is what the field expects from an unbalanced factorial, and what
   `emmeans` is consistent with.
:::

**And the honest caveat.** Type III main effects in the presence of a
real interaction are tests of averaged-over effects that may describe no
actual group. We report them, then go to simple effects.
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: callout-note
**📖 When Type II is the better answer**

If the interaction is **not** significant and you are willing to say the
effects are additive, Type II is more powerful — it does not waste
adjustment on a term you have decided is noise.

Some statisticians argue for always dropping a non-significant
interaction and refitting. That is defensible. Deciding *after* seeing
the *p*-value is less so.
:::

::: callout-tip
**🖐 On a balanced design**

All three are identical, and the whole argument evaporates. That is the
real reason to balance a design when you can.
:::
:::
:::::

## Part 6 · `emmeans`, Four Ways {.divider}

## Way 1 — Marginal Means {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
```{r twa-redux-13}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
emmeans(cray_model, ~ range)
```

```{r twa-redux-14}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
cray_df %>%
  group_by(range) %>%
  summarise(raw_mean = round(mean(growth_per_day), 4)) %>%
  as.data.frame()
```
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
**EMM** 0.2287 and 0.2751 → difference **0.0464**
**Raw** 0.2284 and 0.2697 → difference **0.0413**

::: callout-note
**📖 The raw mean understates it by 12%**

The raw Invasive mean is pulled down because 20 of the 54 Invasive
crayfish were in Papoose, the worst lake. The EMM averages the three
lakes **equally**, so it is not contaminated by where the animals
happened to survive.

Milder than the penguin toy — but in the same direction, for the same
reason.
:::

::: callout-warning
**⚠️ Read the NOTE R prints**

*"Results may be misleading due to involvement in interactions."* That
is not boilerplate. It is `emmeans` telling you this number describes
no lake.
:::
:::
:::::

## Way 2 — Simple Effects, `range` Within Each Lake {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r twa-redux-15}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
pairs(emmeans(cray_model, ~ range | lake))
```

The `|` means **"separately within each level of"**. This is the
analysis the significant interaction sent you to.
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: callout-important
**This is the actual result of the study**

- **Big** — Invasive faster by 0.070, *p* < 0.0001
- **High** — faster by 0.072, *p* < 0.0001
- **Papoose** — 0.003, *p* = **0.78**

Two lakes show a large invasive advantage; the third shows nothing.

Write *this*, not the main effect.
:::

::: callout-tip
**🖐 No multiplicity adjustment appears**

Each lake has only **one** comparison (2 levels → 1 pair), so there is
nothing to adjust within a lake. Across the three families, `emmeans`
leaves it to you.
:::
:::
:::::

## Way 3 — Turn It Around: `lake` Within Each Range {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r twa-redux-16}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
pairs(emmeans(cray_model, ~ lake | range))
```
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: callout-important
**A difference of *magnitude*, not of sign**

Papoose is worse than Big and High **in both ranges** — lake did not
stop mattering. The Papoose deficit is **0.059 / 0.064** for Native and
**0.132 / 0.139** for Invasive: more than twice as costly. Big vs. High
is n.s. in both (*p* = 0.96, 0.79).
:::

::: callout-note
**📖 Same 2 df, two readings**

Way 2: "the invasive advantage disappears in Papoose."
Way 3: "Papoose penalises invasive crayfish twice as hard."

Both correct. Pick the one that answers your question. Tukey **does**
appear here — 3 levels give 3 pairs.
:::
:::
:::::

## Way 4 — The Interaction Contrast {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r twa-redux-17}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
contrast(emmeans(cray_model, ~ range * lake),
         interaction = c("pairwise", "pairwise"))
```

A **difference of differences**: is the range gap in lake X different
from the range gap in lake Y?
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: callout-important
**This localises the interaction**

Big vs. High **0.0023, *p* = 0.90**; Big vs. Papoose −0.073,
*p* = 0.0004; High vs. Papoose −0.076, *p* < 0.0001.

The 2-df interaction is **entirely Papoose**. `Anova()` said *an*
interaction exists; this says **which cells it lives in** — the only one
of the four ways that does.
:::

::: callout-tip
**🖐 The sentence to report**

"The interaction was driven by Papoose Lake, where the invasive
advantage was 0.073–0.076 mm/day smaller than in the other two lakes
(both *p* < 0.001), which did not differ (*p* = 0.90)."
:::
:::
:::::

## And the Picture: `emmip()` {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r twa-redux-18}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 4.6
#| fig-height: 2.9
#| fig-alt: "Interaction plot from emmip showing model estimated marginal means with 95% confidence bands for native and invasive crayfish across Big, High and Papoose lakes; the two lines are far apart and roughly parallel at Big and High and meet at Papoose where the confidence bands overlap completely."
emmip(cray_model, range ~ lake, CIs = TRUE) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9)
```
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: callout-note
**📖 Why `emmip` and not your own `ggplot`**

It plots the **model's** means with intervals from the model's standard
errors. A `ggplot` of raw cell means plots something slightly
different — on an unbalanced design those are not the same numbers.

For the final figure in a paper, build it yourself from
`as.data.frame(emmeans(...))` so you control every element — but check
it against `emmip()` first.
:::

::: callout-tip
**🖐 Read the overlap, not the lines**

At Papoose the two intervals sit on top of each other. At Big and High
they do not come close. That is the interaction, drawn.
:::
:::
:::::

## Why There Are No Planned Comparisons Today

::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
A **planned comparison** is a specific contrast you commit to *before*
seeing the data, because theory demands it. It costs no multiplicity
penalty, because you did not go looking.

This design cannot support one:

- `range` has **2 levels**. There is only one possible comparison, so
  "planned" and "post-hoc" are the same test.
- `lake` has 3 levels but they are **unordered nuisance environments**.
  There is no a priori reason to pit Big against High rather than
  against Papoose.
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: callout-note
**📖 Where they will fit**

You need a factor whose levels have **structure** — a dose gradient, a
control-vs-all-treatments comparison, an ordered sequence.

The urchin density gradient (0 / 33 / 66 / 100%) is the natural case: a
**linear trend** contrast is a single df that asks the real biological
question, instead of six pairwise tests that do not.
:::

::: callout-tip
**🖐 Preview of the syntax**

`contrast(emm, list(linear = c(-3, -1, 1, 3)))`, with the weights
summing to zero. We will build these properly later.
:::
:::
:::::

## Part 7 · Effect Size, Assumptions, Reporting {.divider}

## How Big, Not Just Whether {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r twa-redux-19}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
eta_squared(Anova(cray_model, type = 3))
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.compact-table}
| Term | partial η² | label |
|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| `range` | 0.33 | large |
| `lake` | **0.70** | large |
| `range:lake` | 0.25 | large |
:::

::: callout-important
**`lake` is the biggest effect in the study**

Partial η² = 0.70 for a factor nobody was interested in. The
*experimental* factor, `range`, gets 0.33.

Model $R^2$ = **0.80**. For field ecology that is extraordinary — and
most of it is "which lake did this animal happen to live in."
:::

::: callout-tip
**🖐 This is the number for the next study**

If `lake` carries 0.70 of the explainable variation, a design with
**more lakes** beats one with more crayfish per lake. The *p*-values
could not have told you that.
:::
:::
:::::

## Diagnostics

::::: columns
::: {.column width="58%"}
```{r twa-redux-20}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 5.2
#| fig-height: 3.2
#| fig-alt: "Three diagnostic panels for the crayfish model: a normal Q-Q plot whose upper tail bends sharply away from the line, a residuals-versus-fitted plot showing a wider band of residuals at higher fitted values, and a scale-location style plot of absolute residuals by cell confirming the smallest cells also have the smallest spread."
aug <- tibble(f = fitted(cray_model),
              r = residuals(cray_model),
              rs = rstandard(cray_model))

d_qq <- ggplot(aug, aes(sample = rs)) +
  stat_qq(size = 0.8) + stat_qq_line() +
  labs(title = "Normal Q-Q", x = "Theoretical", y = "Std. residual") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 8)

d_rf <- ggplot(aug, aes(f, r)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, size = 0.9) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  labs(title = "Residuals vs. Fitted", x = "Fitted", y = "Residual") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 8)

d_sd <- cray_cells %>%
  ggplot(aes(n, sd, color = range)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_color_viridis_d(option = "D", end = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "Cell SD vs. cell n", x = "n", y = "SD") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 8) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

(d_qq + d_rf) / d_sd
```
:::

::: {.column width="42%"}
::: callout-warning
**⚠️ Both assumptions fail**

`shapiro.test` on the residuals gives *p* = **0.0043**; `leveneTest` on
the six cells gives *p* = **0.013**.

The Q-Q plot shows why: one crayfish grew 9.25 → 40 mm in 70 days, a
standardised residual of **3.8**.

And cell SDs run 0.008 (Native/Papoose) to 0.046 (Invasive/High) — a
**six-fold** spread, with the biggest variance in the fastest-growing
cells.
:::

::: callout-tip
**🖐 Positive mean-variance relationship**

Spread rising with the mean is the signature of a response that wants a
**log** scale. Next slide.
:::
:::
:::::

## Does the Violation Change the Answer? {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
Three independent ways to ask. The interaction *F*, each way:

```{r twa-redux-21}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
m_log  <- lm(log(growth_per_day) ~ range * lake, data = cray_df)
m_noout <- lm(growth_per_day ~ range * lake,
              data = cray_df[-which.max(abs(rstandard(cray_model))), ])
m_hc3  <- Anova(cray_model, type = 3, white.adjust = "hc3")

tibble(
  approach = c("as fitted", "log(growth)", "outlier dropped",
               "HC3 robust SEs"),
  interaction_F = round(c(Anova(cray_model, type = 3)["range:lake", "F value"],
                          Anova(m_log, type = 3)["range:lake", "F value"],
                          Anova(m_noout, type = 3)["range:lake", "F value"],
                          m_hc3["range:lake", "F"]), 2)
) %>% as.data.frame()
```

And the log model's assumptions: Shapiro *p* = **0.37** (was 0.004),
Levene *p* = **0.053** (was 0.013).
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
::: callout-important
**✅ Every route gives the same conclusion**

Three main effects and an interaction, all strongly significant, with
the interaction *F* between 12.7 and 27.6.

The log transform **fixes normality outright** and nearly fixes
homogeneity, and changes nothing about what you conclude.
:::

::: callout-note
**📖 What to actually report**

Report the **log-scale model** — it is the one whose assumptions hold —
and state that the untransformed analysis gave the same conclusions.

That sentence is worth more than a passed Shapiro test. "The assumption
failed, here are three checks, the answer is stable" is what robustness
means.
:::
:::
:::::

## Reporting It

::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
::: callout-note
**How to report this result**

"Daily growth rate differed between native and invasive crayfish
(two-way ANOVA on log-transformed growth, Type III SS; *F*~1,78~ = 34.2,
*p* < 0.001) and among lakes (*F*~2,78~ = 124.7, *p* < 0.001), and the
two factors interacted (*F*~2,78~ = 13.2, *p* < 0.001; partial η² =
0.25).

Invasive crayfish grew faster than native crayfish in Big
(+0.070 mm d⁻¹, *p* < 0.001) and High (+0.072, *p* < 0.001) lakes but
not in Papoose (+0.003, *p* = 0.78); the interaction contrast confirmed
Papoose differed from both other lakes (*p* ≤ 0.0004) while Big and High
did not differ (*p* = 0.90).

Native and invasive animals were deployed in different windows
(106–108 vs. 70 days, mean temperature 22.0 vs. 23.8 °C), so the range
effect is not a clean genotypic contrast."
:::
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: callout-important
**✅ Four things that must be in it**

1. **Which SS type** — otherwise the reader cannot reproduce you
2. **The interaction before the main effects**, and the simple effects
   that unpack it
3. **An effect size**, not just *p*
4. **The confound**, in the methods, unprompted
:::

::: callout-warning
**⚠️ What a weaker version would say**

*"Invasive crayfish grew significantly faster than native crayfish
(p < 0.001)."* True, and it hides that this is false in one of the three
lakes studied.
:::
:::
:::::

## Part 8 · Wrap-Up {.divider}

## What You Did Today

::::::: columns
:::: {.column width="58%"}
- Ran the **same factorial ANOVA** as last session on data that is
  genuinely unbalanced, and watched the choices start to matter
- Read `Anova(type = 3)` **row by row** — every df accounted for, and
  the interaction row read **first**
- Read `summary()` **line by line** and found the four missing
  coefficients, then **reconstructed a cell mean by hand** to 6 decimals
- Saw the intercept is the mean of **cell means**, not of the data
- Watched `lake`'s *F* fall from **121 (Type I) to 90 (Type III)**, and
  Type I change when you reorder the formula
- Used `emmeans` **four ways** — marginal, simple effects both
  directions, and the **interaction contrast** that localised the effect
  to Papoose
- Failed two assumption tests and then **showed the answer was stable**
::::

:::: {.column width="42%"}
::: callout-important
**✅ The one idea to keep**

A significant interaction **demotes every main effect to a conditional
statement.** The table tells you an interaction exists; only the simple
effects and the interaction contrast tell you *what it is*.

Here: the invasive crayfish growth advantage is real, large, and
**absent in one of the three lakes tested**. No single *p*-value in the
ANOVA table says that.
:::

::: callout-note
**📖 Up next**

What happens when the thing on the right-hand side is **continuous** —
and when `lake` would be better as a **random** effect than a fixed one.
:::
::::

## Readings

::::::: columns
:::: {.column width="55%"}
- **Whitlock & Schluter**, Ch. 18 — factorial designs and interactions.
- **Gotelli & Ellison**, Ch. 10 — two-factor ANOVA and the
  interpretation of interaction terms.
- **Quinn & Keough** (2002), *Experimental Design and Data Analysis for
  Biologists*, Ch. 9 — unbalanced factorial designs and the sums-of-squares
  types. §9.2 is the reference for the Type I/II/III argument in Part 5.
- Sargent, L. W., & Lodge, D. M. (2014). Evolution of invasive traits in
  nonindigenous species: increased survival and faster growth in
  invasive populations of rusty crayfish (*Orconectes rusticus*).
  *Evolutionary Applications, 7*(8), 949–961.
